task.description:
Resolve ISS-0209. `HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md` section 2 gives every handoff a `result.git_evidence.commit_sha_list`. A completing agent fills it in and THEN commits the handoff, so the commit carrying that handoff into git can never appear in the list inside it -- nor can any later correction to the same file. The field is therefore structurally incomplete on every run, and nothing in the protocol says so, leaving a reader unable to distinguish that from careless filling. The finding is stated first-hand by the REVIEWER that raised it, in `handoffs/WF03-ISS0207-20260821/step-03b-reviewer-gate.json` `result.issues` (third entry); `docs/issues/ISS-0209.yaml` carries ORCH's filing and names two candidate directions.

THE DECISION IS YOURS AND IT IS GENUINELY OPEN. ORCH is not prescribing it. The issue names two directions -- make the sha write-back an explicit protocol step, or declare handoff-own commits out of the field's scope -- and you may also reach a third that satisfies the acceptance criteria better. What you may NOT do is leave a reader unable to tell what the list covers.

WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER:

1. MEASURE THE ACTUAL GAP FIRST, because the two directions have different costs and the corpus is what tells you which. Over every JSON file under `handoffs/` other than `registry.json`, determine how many carry a non-empty `commit_sha_list`, how many are empty, and -- for a sample you choose and state -- whether the shas listed are the step's *content* commits, its *own* handoff commit (impossible by the argument above, so a hit here means something else is going on and is worth reporting), or a mixture. Also count how often ORCH's ad hoc write-back pattern actually ran: commits whose subject records a sha into `git_evidence` (`git log --oneline` over `handoffs/` will surface them; the ISS-0201, ISS-0204 and ISS-0207 runs are known instances). Quote your commands. The point is to learn whether the write-back is an established practice worth codifying or an occasional one worth dropping.

2. CHECK THE INFINITE-REGRESS CLAIM RATHER THAN INHERITING IT. The issue asserts that a follow-up write-back commit cannot record itself either, so the regress never terminates. Confirm or refute that against how the write-back commits on those three runs were actually made. If it terminates in practice -- for instance because the write-back records only the PRECEDING commit and nobody expects it to record itself -- then the regress is a red herring and the honest fix is smaller than the issue implies. Say which.

3. DECIDE, and state the reasoning in `result.summary` rather than only the outcome. Weigh: what a reader actually needs the field for; whether the write-back's cost (an extra commit per run, and an ORCH remembering to make it) buys enough; and the weak-model constraint in `core-directives.md` -- a step that depends on an agent remembering an unwritten convention is the class of thing this project keeps having to fix.

4. APPLY it in ONE place, with pointers if others need to refer to it. Section 2 is the natural home since that is where the schema lives. Do not restate the ruling in `ORCHESTRATOR.md` or `core-directives.md`; check `GIT_MERGE.md` too, since it owns the git step that produces most of these shas, and if it needs to point at the ruling, a pointer is what it gets.

5. SCOPE THE RULING TO NEW HANDOFFS. Existing files are not backfilled -- section 4.1(b)'s no-backfill rule is the governing precedent, and the corpus is evidence. Whatever you decide, say from when it applies, and prefer a commit-scoped boundary over a date-scoped one: section 4.1(b) itself explains why a same-day boundary was false in that case, and that reasoning applies here.

6. CLOSE the issue (WF-03 Step 5, taken within this step): `docs/issues/ISS-0209.yaml` gets `status: resolved`, `resolved_in_run: WF03-ISS0209-20260821`, `resolved_at:` from a real clock read. Close GH#400 with `gh issue close 400 --comment "..."` naming this run and the issue file.

7. COMMIT `docs/` and your own handoff file. Do NOT write `handoffs/registry.json` or `handoffs/orchestrator.log` -- both are ORCH's.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Docs-only run. Do not touch `lib/`, `priv/repo/migrations/`, `test/` or `web/`.
- Two other issues are open against the SAME section 1.2 and must be left alone: ISS-0206 (no threshold for 'immediately' in section 1.2 step 2's exception branch; the unclosed loop where section 1 step 3 tells an agent to report a null `started_at` while section 1.2 forbids backfilling it) and ISS-0208 (section 1.2's as-of marker embeds a running list of re-run readings that is stale by construction). Your target is section 2's `git_evidence`, not section 1.2 at all. If your fix seems to require touching section 1.2, stop and report it rather than reaching into another issue's scope.
- Your `result.status` must be one of PASS/FAIL/PARTIAL/BLOCKED/SKIPPED. The previous run's step 03 set it to COMPLETED, which is a top-level `status` value and not legal there; the correction cost an extra commit.
- Timestamps come from the clock at the moment you write each one. Read the clock in its OWN command, then write -- never batch `date -u` and the write that consumes it into one shell command; see the first entry in `docs/anti-patterns.md`.
- Your handoff's `started_at` was stamped by ORCH at dispatch, per section 1.2. Do not touch it. Claim by setting `status` to `IN_PROGRESS` only.
acceptance_criteria: Section 2 states explicitly what commit_sha_list does and does not cover, so a reader can tell structural incompleteness from careless filling

If the write-back becomes a protocol step, it is written concretely enough that a weak agent performs it every time, and its own unrecordability is acknowledged rather than left as an infinite regress
If handoff-own commits are declared out of scope instead, the field keeps a stated purpose -- what it IS for -- rather than becoming decorative
The chosen direction is stated in exactly one place, with pointers elsewhere, per the one-canonical-statement property ISS-0204 established
Existing handoff files are not backfilled; the ruling is scoped to new handoffs with a commit-scoped boundary, per section 4.1(b) precedent
The corpus was measured first-hand -- how many handoffs carry a non-empty commit_sha_list, how many are empty, and how often the ad hoc write-back commit actually ran -- with the commands quoted
The issue's infinite-regress claim is confirmed or refuted against how the write-back commits were actually made, rather than inherited from the issue text
docs/issues/ISS-0209.yaml carries status: resolved, resolved_in_run and a clock-read resolved_at; GH#400 is closed
Section 1.2 is untouched and ISS-0206's and ISS-0208's subject matter is not taken; no file outside docs/ and handoffs/WF03-ISS0209-20260821/ is modified

result.summary: ISS-0209 resolved in HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md section 2, in one new subsection: 'result.git_evidence.commit_sha_list -- what it covers, and what it structurally cannot'. All seven numbered steps executed in order; all nine acceptance criteria met. (1) CORPUS MEASURED FIRST-HAND, BEFORE DECIDING. Command: a python heredoc from the repo root walking `handoffs/`.rglob('*.json') excluding registry.json, json.loads on each, reading result.git_evidence.commit_sha_list. RESULT: 610 files, 0 unparseable; 276 carry a NON-EMPTY list, 261 carry an EMPTY list, and 73 have no result.git_evidence.commit_sha_list key at all (the pre-field flat-schema files). 502 shas are recorded in total. CLASSIFIED BY CENSUS, NOT BY SAMPLE -- for every one of the 502 I ran `git show --name-only --pretty=format: <sha>` and tested whether the listing handoff's own path appeared in the touched set. 284 (57%) are UNRESOLVABLE -- `git cat-file -t` returns non-zero, the object is not in this repository. Of the 218 that resolve (209 after dropping 9 malformed non-sha strings), 94 name a commit that touched THE VERY FILE THAT LISTS THEM, 34 are content-only, 39 mixed content+handoff, 42 other-handoff-only. (2) THE '94 SELF-HITS' FINDING, WHICH THE ISSUE'S ARGUMENT SAYS IS IMPOSSIBLE, AND WHAT IT ACTUALLY MEANS. It is not impossible and it is not something else going on: it is the write-back, visible in the corpus. A file cannot contain the sha of the commit that creates it, but a LATER commit can edit the file to add it -- so a self-hit is exactly the fingerprint of a sha written back after the fact. I traced each with `git log -S<sha> -- <file>`; 8 of the earliest-introducing commits are explicit `chore(...): record ... sha in ... git_evidence` commits, and the remainder resolve to squash-merge commits (`(#128)`, `(#80)`) where the branch history that would distinguish write-back from ordering has been collapsed and I therefore state the limit rather than over-claim. (3) THE 284 DEAD SHAS ARE THE FINDING THAT CHANGED THE ANSWER, AND THE MECHANISM IS PROTOCOL-MANDATED, NOT INFERRED. `GIT_MERGE.md` step 5 is `git rebase origin/main` (replays every commit under a new sha) and step 8 is `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch` (collapses the branch into one new commit and discards it). Corroborated on `main`: `git log --oneline | grep -c '(#[0-9]*)'` = 175 squash commits against `git log --merges --oneline | wc -l` = 15 true merges, and a worked case -- WF02-REQ042-20260817's recorded c1a4c2e... is absent while its work is on main as 84a0dab '(#123)'. So MOST recorded shas are already dead by the time anyone reads them, and the field's audit value for merged work is largely spent regardless of how carefully it is filled. (4) REGRESS CLAIM: REFUTED, against how the write-back commits were actually made. `git log --oneline --all -- handoffs/` filtered on git_evidence/sha subjects returns 23 commits, of which 21 are genuine write-backs (2 are false positives matching 'shape'). They span 12 of the 63 run directories -- and 7 of the 21 are a single run, WF02-REQ049 -- so this was never established practice. `git show` on each: every one changes exactly one handoff file, `"commit_sha_list": []` -> the ONE preceding commit's sha, and stops. I then tested whether any of the 21 is itself recorded anywhere in the corpus: ZERO are (the one apparent hit, 25440db, is a 'shape anomalies' subject false positive, not a write-back). The regress the issue posits has never occurred and terminates at depth 1 by construction, because nobody expects a write-back to record itself. The honest residue is EXACTLY ONE unrecorded commit per run -- much smaller than the issue implies. (5) DECISION AND REASONING. I took the issue's SECOND direction -- state the scope -- rather than making the write-back a protocol step, and I widened it with the two findings above that the issue did not have. Against making it mandatory: it costs an extra commit per run; it is the class of step that depends on an agent remembering an unwritten convention, which `core-directives.md`'s weak-model constraint says this project keeps having to fix; and by finding (3) what the extra commit buys is usually a reference the next rebase or squash invalidates within the hour. Against leaving it silent: a reader could not distinguish structural incompleteness from careless filling, which is the issue's actual complaint and is answered by writing it down, at zero recurring cost. So the field KEEPS a stated purpose rather than becoming decorative -- it is a convenience pointer to the commits this step produced, explicitly NOT the audit trail, with `git log --oneline -- handoffs/<run_id>/` named as authoritative where they disagree -- and the subsection states what an empty list means (this step committed nothing beyond its own handoff, never 'the agent forgot'), what a non-empty one means (these were this step's commits at the moment of writing, never 'all the run's commits' and never 'these still resolve'), and that an unresolvable sha means a rebased or squashed branch rather than a careless agent. (6) ONE PLACE, POINTERS ELSEWHERE. The ruling lives only in section 2. `GIT_MERGE.md` gets a six-line note under step 8 that names its own two steps as the invalidating mechanism and points at section 2 with 'this line does not restate it'. Nothing was added to `ORCHESTRATOR.md` or `core-directives.md`; `grep -rn commit_sha_list docs/ .claude/` returned only the section 2 schema fence before this run. (7) SCOPE AND NO BACKFILL. Items 1-3 describe properties the field always had, so the READING binds handoffs of any age; only FILLING is boundary-scoped, at commit `12f8f4c`, per section 4.1(b)'s commit-not-date precedent (42 of 46 same-day files fell on the wrong side there). The 276 handoffs already carrying a list are NOT backfilled and no write-back is owed on any of them. (8) THE IRONY, MADE LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN LEFT AS A JOKE. A boundary must name a literal sha to be mechanical for a weak agent, and `12f8f4c` could not contain its own -- item 1 applying to a doc instead of a handoff. So I committed the subsection (12f8f4c) and then wrote its sha in with a second commit (389eb0b), and the subsection says so in a closing paragraph: that is the one case where the write-back earns its extra commit, and 389eb0b records only its predecessor and is recorded nowhere, exactly as the ruling instructs. This handoff demonstrates the same thing from the other side: the list below carries the two docs commits and structurally cannot carry the commit that commits this file. (9) BOUNDARIES HELD. `git diff --numstat` on HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md before commit read 77/0 -- INSERTIONS-ONLY, which is mechanical proof that section 1.2 was not touched and that ISS-0206's and ISS-0208's subject matter was not taken; the new subsection sits between the `context.requirement_text` paragraph and 'What goes in task.description'. Nothing outside `docs/` and this run's handoff directory was modified. `handoffs/registry.json` and `handoffs/orchestrator.log` are ORCH's, remain uncommitted at 20/0 and 6/0 deletions, and I did not open either for edit. `result.status` is PASS -- a legal section 2 value, not the COMPLETED that cost the previous run an extra commit. Both timestamps came from `date -u` issued as its own command with the write as a separate later call, per the first entry in `docs/anti-patterns.md`; `started_at` (10:48:13Z, ORCH's dispatch stamp) was not touched and the claim was status -> IN_PROGRESS only.

issues.description: Corpus finding worth its own issue, discovered while measuring for ISS-0209 and deliberately not fixed here. 284 of the 502 shas recorded in handoffs (57%) no longer resolve to any object in this repository, because GIT_MERGE.md step 5 rebases and step 8 squash-merges away the branch shas agents record. The new section 2 subsection tells a READER how to interpret that, which closes ISS-0209 -- but it does not give a WRITER anything better to record. Candidate follow-on: have GIT_MERGE.md step 10 record the post-merge squash commit sha (which does survive) in the Step Final handoff's git_evidence, so each run retains one durable pointer instead of a set of dead branch shas. That is a change to what agents write, not to how the field is read, so it belongs in its own run with its own gate.

Schema-hygiene finding, not acted on. Of the 502 recorded shas, 9 are not sha-shaped strings at all (they fail a hex/length test), and 73 of the 610 handoff files have no result.git_evidence.commit_sha_list key -- the same pre-field flat-schema files section 4.1(b) and section 3 already count in other contexts (the two step-00-git-setup files among them). Neither is a defect this run introduced and neither is backfillable, but if ISS-0191's linter is extended, the field's value shape is a cheap thing for it to assert going forward.

result.next_action: ORCH: close the run. Two docs commits (12f8f4c, 389eb0b) plus this handoff's own commit are local and unpushed. GH#400 is already closed with a comment naming this run and 12f8f4c; docs/issues/ISS-0209.yaml reads status: resolved with a clock-read resolved_at. Release queue task 209 and commit handoffs/registry.json and handoffs/orchestrator.log (yours, still uncommitted, append-only clean at 20/0 and 6/0 -- I did not touch them). File the two MINORs above as follow-on issues; the first is the substantive one and is the natural next run against this field. Note that per the ruling just landed, the commit carrying this file is structurally absent from the list above and no write-back is owed on it -- if ORCH makes one anyway it is optional, records only that commit, and is not itself recorded.
